utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, February 16th, 2010, and I greet everyone here; first our witness, General Petkovic, the accused, Defence counsel, all members of the OTP, and everyone helping us. I believe Mr. Scott wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly, I hope. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to each of Your Honours, Counsel, all those helping us around the courtroom. Just two procedural matters, Your Honour, really about scheduling. First, the Chamber may recall that there are a number of motions, I believe, outstanding in connection with the proposed 92 ter witnesses of the Coric Defence. The questions relate to the amount of time to be taken for examination -- courtroom examination by various -- not just the Prosecution, but various of the parties, including some of the co-accused. We're now a little bit more than halfway through the month of February. It becomes, Your Honours, very difficult for anyone to make schedule or calender the month of March without knowing more about the -- I'm been signaled to slow down. Sorry, Judge Prandler. Let me rephrase the last part. I believe it's in everyone's interest, certainly the Prosecution's, certainly, well, I believe, the Chamber's and the Defence, to be able to plan everyone's calendars and schedules. Since we don't know how much time will be allocated for each of the witnesses, it's virtually impossible to sit down with a calender and try to plan out the month, so we just simply bring that forward a bit to the Chamber's attention. It would be helpful if we could get some further guidance from the Chamber on those matters, because that first witness will appear in approximately two weeks or so. That's point number 1, Your Honour. A second scheduling point. The Chamber may recall that some weeks ago, Mr. Karnavas raised the question of the Easter recess. The Chamber had at least preliminarily indicated a plan to take some break toward the end of April. Mr. Karnavas, quite rightly, in my view, raised the question of how that might affect or not an Easter break, and the Chamber had taken that under advisement. But, again, I don't think, unless I'm mistaken, that there's been any further direction on that. Of course, the Chamber can maintain the schedule it announced. We all understand that. But I hope the Chamber will also understand -- I think I can speak for the Defence, perhaps rarely, but maybe on this occasion, people would like to plan personal and family schedules and holidays. So if the Chamber might be minded to give us a bit more guidance on that, that would be appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Since we're dealing with procedural matters, first of all, Mr. Scott certainly speaks for me on that last point. I can't speak for anybody else. I wasn't going to raise this point, but could I just ask for some technical assistance, because I'm not getting my LiveNote. That's just since I decided to stand up and say something. But, no, what I'm asking for, Your Honour, you may recall the other day we asked for -- the Petkovic asked for and were given leave to reply to a response from the Coric Defence in relation to our application for additional time to cross-examine viva voce witnesses. We've since put in a motion to ask for additional time to cross-examine their 92 ter witnesses or four of their 92 ter witnesses. We have a response. In a similar way, Your Honour, a couple of points do arise which we would like to deal with by way of reply. I notified -- I'm not saying she agreed, but I notified Coric counsel that I would be making this application. Your Honour, it's ready. We could file it today. It's pretty short. I ask for leave to put in a reply under Rule 126 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, you're asking for additional time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what our motion asks for, Your Honour, but that's -- as with the viva voce witnesses, where we got to, our motion for additional time, the Coric response was filed on, well, Sunday or Monday, and we are now asking for leave to reply, which, of course, we do need. And that's ready to file, and then Your Honours will have the complete batch of pleadings on that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask my colleagues whether they agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, everyone agrees for once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should say thank you, plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues from the OTP and from the Defence teams. Good afternoon, Mr. Petkovic, and good afternoon to everybody who's with us. Before we continue our examination, I ask for your leave, Your Honours, to address you for two or three minutes with the following request. Yesterday, after approximately one hour of examining Mr. Petkovic about what he learned about combat activities in the areas of Sovici and Doljani and about the burning of some Muslim houses a few days subsequently, about how he drafted the report for the commander-in-chief, about how he spoke to the supreme commander about the events at Sovici and Doljani, and about this being a topic for discussion between the delegations of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia in Zagreb on the 24th and 25th of April, 1993, the meeting was held in the presence of the co-chairman for the former Yugoslavia, and in that context, finally, a meeting at Citluk was mentioned, a meeting of the highest bodies of Herceg-Bosna, on the 29th of April, 1993. After dealing with all this, I tried to sum up Mr. Petkovic's answers, upon which the OTP objected to this. Since I and everybody else in this courtroom know that Mr. Scott is very familiar with this case, and there is no doubt that Mr. Scott would raise an issue merely to interrupt the examination, so I believe that his objection was sincere, and that prompted me to wonder what was wrong about my intention. And my analysis of the transcript showed the following: The objective of my examination of Mr. Petkovic had totally disappeared after a series of questions asked by the Judges, so that it was very difficult to conclude what the Defence tries to argue and what the crucial positions of the Defence are with regard to the topics the Defence chose to present to the Judges, considering them being the most important ones. As we are pleading our case for your sake, Your Honours, so that you may get to know General Petkovic and so that you may ask him as many questions as you want, including questions of your choice, whichever questions you want, I would like to suggest to you to find a compromise. It is the interest of the Defence to clearly and continuously present their case, enabling also you, Your Honours, to ask questions about any topic. That's why I ask your leave to allow us to complete our examination about an individual topic. All topics we want to deal with are mentioned at the beginning of the first binder. The topics are separated by coloured sheets of paper, and a heading can be found at the beginning of each such tab, so I believe there will be no problem for you to return to any topic if you should consider it necessary to clarify it, additionally -- and if you should like to additionally examine General Petkovic about any of these topics. So I ask you to be permitted to complete my examination about a certain topic without Your Honours asking questions, whereupon you will have the chance to ask any questions you like, and the Petkovic Defence certainly will not object to that. And one more thing. We have established that 20 to 25 per cent of the time are used for follow-up questions to the questions of the Judges. That is why we decided not to put any follow-up questions during our examination-in-chief, but, rather, anything that we consider very important will be left for our redirect examination. I would now ask you, Your Honours, to consider this proposal, and if you should deem it rational or well-founded, then I would like to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't discussed this among Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Could I just add -- I didn't want to interrupt my lead counsel, but the problem with LiveNote is reasonably widespread. I know there are several others in the court who are not able to get to LiveNote, and we must stress, Your Honour, it is a really vital tool for us to -- apparently the problem is a bit more widespread even than I thought, it affects the other side, so I'm now speaking for them, after they've spoken for me. What a nice day, anyway, apart from the difficulty with the LiveNote, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, you need LiveNote. I don't need LiveNote, but everyone works the way they want to. Now, as to Ms. Alaburic's application, it's an important one. I note that because Mr. Scott had not understood the Defence case, that he put questions, you know, and then the Judges are victim to this, and I can agree to that. You know, when I put a question, I always do that from a document, because the document is part and parcel of the question. And so coming back after that to that, that's a problem. So, personally, I cannot agree with what you are saying and what you're proposing. However, I do congratulate you on the excellence of your file. It's extremely well organised, according to different topics, and the document you gave us on the dates is absolutely excellent because it really helps us follow the events. When you talked about this meeting held with the representatives of the international community after Sovici-Doljani, I looked at your document, and I saw traces of all this. So it's really well made. Thank you. Now, as far as I'm concerned, I will try to refrain from interrupting you during your demonstration. I'll do my best, but I can't guarantee that when there's a document that sounds -- that looks essential -- and you know that all the questions that I put to the witness now are -- you know, we're almost at the end of the trial now, so all my questions are core questions, they go to the core of the matter, and I think it would be a pity if I had to wait for the end of everything, because anything can happen in the meanwhile and I can just forget my question and not put it, whereas it's an essential question. But I'll do my best. I promise I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I want to react, because I do not want it to appear as if it was only Mr. Antonetti who asks a lot of questions, because I have been rather active during your examination, too. And I think it is not really possible to put stringent restraints on the Judges, but I have, as I have stated before, full understanding for your plight, and I will also try to refrain from asking questions prematurely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you very much for your understanding, and I wish to reiterate that it is certainly not my intention to prevent you from asking questions which you consider necessary, because what we're doing here, we're doing for you. So we appreciate your interest and your desire to clarify all details, because that's the very reason why we're here. I suggest that we continue our examination, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the agreement of the Judges. You know, my fellow Judge and myself are going to try to do our best not to interrupt you. But let me give you an example. Yesterday, 4D1355 was an interview with General Petkovic. When I saw this document, which we had already seen because it had already been shown, but at the time I hadn't put any questions on this document because I didn't feel that was the right moment to do so. But now, yesterday, when I looked at this document again, and you did not ask any questions -- or the question I wanted to ask, i.e., that General Petkovic has said that an investigation was underway, an investigation carried out by the military prosecutor, I suddenly found out that -- decided that I had to put the question, because it was important; notably, regarding Article 7.3 of the Statute. So I did take the floor when you were talking about something else, that's true, but that's very difficult because I thought it was so important to put this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is absolutely no doubt we fully agree that all these questions are very important, and, frankly speaking, as we have -- as after these four years we know you rather well, we all expect you, actually, to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General -- I've been told that LiveNote still isn't working, but we have the transcript on our center screens, so I believe that we can proceed. General, we were dealing with combat activities in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar is telling me that it should be fixed in about 10 minutes -- within 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Registrar also had an IC number, and he didn't want to forget that. Registrar, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one IC number. The Prosecution has submitted their response to 4D and 2D's objection to their request for admission of documents via Witness 4D-AA. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01178. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I also want to say for the Defence counsel and for the Prosecutor that LiveNote is not effected -- is down in every courtroom, not just this one, but it's a general problem. But normally, within about 10 minutes, it should be up again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if you remember, yesterday we broke off while you were looking at a map of Mostar on the 30th of June, 1993. I'm not going to ask any questions about that map now. I'll do that in the redirect examination. But please let's see map 4D622 now. It's a map of the same area, that is, Mostar and the surrounding areas, after the 30th of June, 1993. Have you found it, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what kind of event is that, due to which the area of Eastern Mostar is connected to the Jablanica area on the left bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this situation came about on the 30th of June, when some elements of the HVO of Muslim ethnicity, aided and abetted by the ABiH, attacked some formations of the HVO to the north and south of Mostar, and, assisted by the ABiH, gained full control over areas in the north of Mostar, thus establishing a corridor with Jablanica and Konjic, and to the south of Mostar establishing a corridor towards Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, based on the maps that we saw yesterday and today, who is enlarging the area under their control in 1993, the ABiH or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is clear from all this that the ABiH was enlarging the territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the OTP claims in the indictment that the combat activities of the HVO in mid-April 1993, are the beginning of the implementation, I quote, "a criminal plan of prosecution, arrest, and eviction of Muslims." In accordance with your understanding of the situation on the ground, is that statement correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that statement is completely false and construed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How would you qualify the activities of the HVO from mid-April 1993 to the end of that year, or even up to the signing of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All activities of the HVO at that time were exclusively of a defensive nature, the purpose being to preserve as much territory inhabited by Croats as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thus we have completed this topic. We'll pass on to another, and that is Sovici and Doljani. Judge Trechsel, yesterday you expressed the wish to ask a question about Sovici and Doljani. That is why I would like to tell you that now I'm about to deal with the evacuation of civilians, because, to my mind, we fully clarified yesterday the issue of combat activities around Sovici and Doljani. So if your question refers to that, I would kindly ask you to put your question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Unless you want to deal with Sovici-Doljani, there is one point in particular in the indictment which refers to persons having been held at the school of Doljani. I wonder if that -- I could imagine that it is in your programme, and I will let you have precedence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, we have a map here on the screen. General Petkovic, this is the situation after June 30th, 1993. I think that's what's on the caption. You will probably remember that Ms. West spent a great deal of time on the roads, trying to see if you could be exposed to fire when you were driving on certain roads. But independently of the roads, according to me, the entire area in green, which is the area controlled by the BH Army, or allegedly, I see that East Mostar is under control, so I have a very straightforward question. A child could put this question to you, actually. There's no need for a judge or a professor to put this question. In this area in green, controlled by the ABiH, could a Muslim citizen, by night, to avoid fire or shots, could this citizen of East Mostar, walking away, could he leave Mostar by foot towards the north, or maybe going towards the south? Would that have been possible? Could you walk away, go by foot, or was it totally impossible because the VRS maybe had night sights on their rifles, on their guns, maybe the HVO had the same thing, so maybe it was impossible not to be hit even at night because of these night-vision rifles? So what can you say to that? Was there a possibility to escape by foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when you speak about walking, it was absolutely possible to move about on foot because there are many paths, and you could reach almost any house on a tarmac road. But nobody has mentioned that the area is an agricultural one in which there are orchards and vineyards, so you may even fail to notice a bus moving down the M-17 road. So I repeat that whoever wanted to go somewhere could walk out of Mostar and go to Jablanica and further without being noticed by anyone or, indeed, harmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And by saying this, you are positive about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying, Yes, in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you can recollect, and it might be complicated, but I was wondering whether you had received reports or information according to which a given civilian could have been killed in the area that is depicted in green on the map during the day or during the night because he or she was fleeing. Did you receive this sort of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had no information about the killing of any civilian along that road from East Mostar running north. We didn't have any such information, nor did any member of the army -- BH Army ever complain, because they contacted UNPROFOR quite frequently, ever complain that any civilian had lost his life along that stretch.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to deal with the topic of Sovici and Doljani as of the 4th of May, 1993. Let's look at a document straight away. 4D447 is the number. This is a report from the chief of the Security Centre of the 44th Mountain Brigade, and his name was Zajko Sihirlic. Tell us, please, General, on the 4th of May were you attending a meeting at Jablanica with a delegation of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, did you agree that an HVO delegation and a BH Army delegation would tour Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was agreed that the destination would be Sovici and Doljani and two others north towards Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The BH Army commanders at the meeting in Jablanica, did they present any information about any crimes committed in the Sovici and Doljani area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gained the impression from them that they couldn't wait to get there, because rumours were going 'round about 1.000 Muslims killed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in the BH Army delegation, was the author of this document one of its members?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the members of the delegation. I remember him because he was with a cameraman, and he just gave the cameraman instructions. He said, Film this, film that. It was a cameraman from army television, but attached to the studio, a television studio in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So he says in this report of his, dated the 4th of May, 1993, that: "For tomorrow, an unconditional evacuation of the civilian population from Doljani and Sovici was agreed." Tell us, please, General, in view of the situation on the ground and your knowledge of the author of this document, is there a single reason why he should use the term "evacuation of the civilian population" if it was a case of any violent expulsion of people from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the author of this document was well aware of the situation. He kept Pasalic and Halilovic, and he also advised and instructed the cameraman as to what he should film.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in Sovici, did you visit the school there in which there were men, younger and old ones, if I remember?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did visit the school in Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on behalf of the BH Army, did the school -- did Halilovic and Pasalic and other commanders visit the school in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both Pasalic, Halilovic, and several other of their men from the Command of the 44th Brigade visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did any of those people say that their houses had been burnt?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of those people did say that their houses had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, General, did those people express the desire to leave Sovici?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I told them that by 4.00 we would allow all those who could to return. A part of them asked temporarily to relocate to Jablanica and wait and see how the situation would develop.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, who agreed -- who reached an agreement with these people to have them evacuated from Sovici?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Arif Pasalic remained with them afterwards, and another man. I can't remember his -- or two other men. I can't remember their names. They stayed with them, once we had left the school. And Pasalic came up to me and Halilovic and said that he wanted to have all the people evacuated towards Jablanica. They separated a bit, stood apart. Halilovic supported this. And so with that, with this position and decision, we set out towards Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, who were you with in the UNPROFOR APC?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halilovic and I were in the UNPROFOR transporter together -- APC together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you discuss the question of the civilians' evacuation from Sovici with Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they'd already reached the decision when they were in front of the school and said that they would evacuate the civilians from Sovici and Doljani. So they were just looking into the ways and means of how to ensure the means for this transportation; buses and so on. So when we left Sovici and Doljani -- actually, while we were waiting to leave, they made this definite decision, said, That's our decision, and will you help us by providing transport for these people because we don't have the necessary number of buses?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what did you do in that respect, General, when you reached Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in Sovici and Doljani, I told Mr. Pula, the commander of our battalion -- or, rather, I asked him whether, at the positions at Sovici and Doljani, there were any free buses. And then from Sovici and Doljani, we called up Mostar to see if they could provide any buses, because the request was for five buses. And the answer we were given was that they would find five buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Halilovic and Pasic [as interpreted], did they expect anything else from you except for the buses? Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was anything else required except for the buses for Sovici and Doljani that they wanted us to procure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's finish with this document. To the best of your knowledge, this observation about an agreement for the secure and safe evacuation of the civilian population from Sovici and Doljani, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I'm taking the floor not to touch upon another issue, but I would like to talk about the school. We talked about that school. I see that in all cases brought before this Tribunal, because as you are aware, I was a Pre-Trial Judge, or I was in other trials as well, I was in confirmation hearings as well, so I watch what is happening. As far as schools are concerned I am struck by the fact that in the former Yugoslavia, when there was a conflict somewhere, civilians, men, women, children, would be gathered together in schools. Everyone did that; the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims. So I was wondering why school buildings were used. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in small places like Sovici and Doljani, if you look at the socially-owned buildings available, there are only schools. In some places, you might find some sort of centre, if the place had something like it - perhaps tourists came in and they had a community centre of some kind - but otherwise all you would find would be a school building in all these small places; nothing else, just the school building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answer is that it was the only building which could host a certain number of people. And as far as you know, was everyone doing the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me put it this way: When I went 'round Central Bosnia with Halilovic on the 20th -- or, rather, the 21st, more than the 20th, mostly in all the places that we stopped by in, you had school buildings, premises, except for one place which was in Kaonik, and they had a gas station there. And in Vitez, you had a cinema called the Partisans Cinema. But all the other places, Kruscica, Podgorica, I can't remember all the names of these small places, all they had was a school building -- a primary school building for the first four classes of primary school. So that would make it five rooms, or possibly four rooms, possibly five.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's look at the next document, which is P2182. This is a document which bears your name on it. It's not signed. Tell us, please, General, before this trial did you ever see this document before that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I never saw this document before. And this document has been placed on its head. It's topsy-turvy, if you look at my name there, because in the upper left-hand corner you wouldn't have a heading like that. And if somebody were to say that it was from the Main Staff, not even the most illiterate person within the Main Staff would have written it up this way. I don't know what all this is and how it was compiled this way. And, secondly, the date that was subsequently written in here, and this alleged letter of mine, would not be needed at all, because I left at 2.00 -- I left Sovici and Doljani. I knew what was going on there. So when I saw this document, I asked myself, Who could have written it, and put my name there, to boot? So I'm afraid that somebody needed this document. Who needed it and for what purpose, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, a question that I would like to put to you, which is not linked to this document. When you were not here, General Praljak testified, and you may have actually been here sometimes. I can't quite recollect. General Praljak argued that some people have produced false documents, and those false documents were actually introduced in the archives. And General Praljak was actually very clear. He said that those who would have any interest in doing so would try to, therefore, not be held responsible. I can't quite remember what he said. But when I heard that, I also made a mental note that I would ask this question to you, so I'm putting this to you now. What do you think? What is your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, a document like this, written in my name, in the Main Staff is a document that nobody could have written that way, because, I mean, just look at the heading. It has nothing whatsoever to do with the Main Staff. Now, in the Herceg Stjepan Brigade -- in the Mijat Tomic Battalion, well, for about two and a half hours or three hours that day, I -- well, I left Mr. Stipe Polo and asked him what had been agreed with Pasalic and Halilovic, and he knew all about it. I asked him about it, and he knew all about it. So there was no logic in writing a document of this kind at all. So that quite simply I, too, feel that somebody needed to write this kind of document and did so. And if you look at it, there's no stamp. It doesn't say which archive it was stored in, where it was found. It has absolutely nothing to indicate that it was the Main Staff, except for the fact that somebody wrote at the bottom "Chief of the HVO Main Staff, Milivoj Petkovic." So as I say, I cannot link this document in any way to the Main Staff, because it has absolutely nothing to do with it, nor were the contents of this document necessary at all. Why write it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you have not answered my question, which was of a different type. I wanted to know whether what had been put forward by General Praljak, namely, that some people, and we don't know who those people would be, some people would have made up false documents and would have introduced those documents in the archives in order for those documents to be then produced in a court of law. Do you think that this may have happened, or do you think that General Praljak has made up false assertions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak is right when he said what he did, and I support him there, especially looking at a document like this. If the document had "Main Staff" as a title, as a heading, then I might even feel that maybe it was a proper document. But written this way, it leads me to believe that it was used for somebody else's interest, and certainly not mine or, least of all, anybody else's in this courtroom, so I consider it to be a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you. Your answer is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, please, the next day, from Sovici and Doljani, was everybody evacuated who wanted to leave or were the military-able men kept back?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, everybody went -- left Sovici when the people -- they were in the school when the decision to evacuate them was made, and they all left the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, General, which is P2203. And this is a question asking whether the buses had been sent, and this question was sent on the 5th of May. General Filip Filipovic said that he was the author of this letter with this question and that it was sent at the beginning of the meeting which was held on the 5th of May, 1993, in Jablanica. Tell us, please, General, is what General Filipovic said correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because on the footage you can see me giving him the number that he was supposed to call.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, at the beginning of the meeting did you have any information at all about the fact that the evacuation had been carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither Halilovic nor I had any information telling us that the evacuation had taken place, and that was strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, P2191. It's a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This relates immediately to this. I probably misunderstood something, because I thought that Mr. Petkovic had said he had called on Mostar for five buses in order to make transport for evacuation possible, and now he says -- you say you didn't know about the evacuation. Can you put me right, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. On the 4th of May, 1993, when we returned from Sovici, Halilovic, Pasalic, and everybody else, upon their request to procure five buses, we called up Mostar from Jablanica and told them to send five buses to Doljani in the morning. When we met again on the following day in the tent of the Spanish Battalion, I believe it was General Pasalic who raised the issue and inquired about the buses. It was then that I gave General Filipovic the number to call, and he put down the number in his notebook. And in a minute or so, he called Mostar and asked whether they had sent the buses. And from Mostar, they sent an urgent dispatch to Jablanica, because we didn't have direct phone communication with Doljani. We had to call Doljani -- sorry, Mostar, and they would call Doljani. That was how we communicated. On the following morning, Pasalic started asking questions about whether or not the buses would come, and I ordered Filipovic to check. And we were all waiting for the buses, but later we saw from the documents that the buses had already evacuated the civilians in the morning without us in Jablanica, that is, Halilovic and me, ever knowing about it, because nobody could call us on the phone from Sovici or Doljani. They couldn't call us up at the UNPROFOR base in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That has fully clarified for me. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, in this document, I'm looking at the B/C/S version. Unfortunately, we only have copies. Sometimes when we have the original, we may have some surprises because we realise that on the flip side there were stamps which do not appear or have not been photocopied. Anyway, this being said, I see that there is a stamp, "Institute for Crime Investigation," or "Investigation for Crimes Against Humanity as International Law, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." I can assume, therefore, that this document was within this institute in charge of investigating those crimes. What do you think, and were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I didn't know that. I read it here, the same way you did. But above that, you see that the source of this document is the TO Staff of Jablanica, so it was the TO Staff that first laid its hands on this document and forwarded it to the Commission for Crime Investigation. Now, the question is how the Jablanica staff came by this document that was sent to the HVO at Sovici and Doljani. I suppose that once the ABiH, in late June and early July, took Sovici and Doljani, they raided the command and took all the documents they found there, all the HVO documents, and that's how this documentation got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us look at the two following documents. The first one is P2191, and this is a report of the president of the HVO of Gornji Vakuf, who says that: "Today," that is, on the 5th of May, 1993, "at 9.00, 300 persons, approximately, were brought to the Sicaja petrol station in Pidris, these persons hailing from Doljani and Sovici." So this is a report of their arrival at Gornji Vakuf at 0900 [realtime transcript read in error "1700"] hours. The next document, 4D458 -- correction, not 1700 hours, 0900 hours, that is, 9:00 a.m. So the report reads that they arrived at Gornji Vakuf at 9.00 in the morning. The following document is 4D458. This is a report of the chief of Staff of the Command of the 4th Corps of the ABiH, Mr. Sulejman Budakovic, who also says that he has a report according to which civilians from Sovici were brought to Gornji Vakuf at 9:00 a.m. It follows from these two documents, General, that the people from Sovici were evacuated early in the morning on the 5th of May and that at 9.00 a.m. they were already at Gornji Vakuf. Did you and Sefer Halilovic, as well as the members of your delegations, have this information when you met at Jablanica on that same day in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We started our meeting at 9.00 and began to speak about the buses, but here we see that the evacuation had already been performed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the commanders of the ABiH agree with the inhabitants of Sovici to be evacuated to Jablanica or Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that they should be evacuated to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now look at a part of a video that we have already seen in this courtroom. It's about the meeting in Jablanica. The document is P2187, 2187. We are going to show you a clip from 42 minutes, 31 seconds, until -- that's the start, 42:31, up until 44 minutes, 7 seconds. As there is no description of the situation in this video-clip, I would like to draw your attention to the following: This is a convoy of UNPROFOR vehicles which, with the delegations of the ABiH and the HVO, went from Jablanica to Doljani, and on the way there they -- there were some obstacles. They couldn't continue until the obstacles were removed. We will show the clip showing how these obstacles were removed. We can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see these obstacles on the road, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was waiting in the APC for the obstacles to be removed, and this was the area of Kosna Luka on the road from Jablanica to Doljani. This was a check-point of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, what happened to that check-point once the UNPROFOR vehicles had passed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The check-point was supposed to be reconstructed into its original state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Whose demand was that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the demand of the ABiH, both those at the check-point and those in our escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When, on the following day, buses transported the people from Sovici toward Jablanica, did they have to take the same road?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only road they could take to go to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the buses couldn't pass by that check-point, what could the bus drivers have done?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had two options, either to return the persons they were driving back to their point of departure or to take the road to Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have seen in the report that the drivers decided to go to Vakuf. Now let's take a look at document 4D1079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is again a question immediately relating to this video. Would it be possible to show the Chamber on a map where this obstacle was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, we can show the location of these obstacles on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would the map of the Jablanica area be suitable, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems that we can use Map 4D2025. I'm merely reminding everybody that this is related to Judge Trechsel's question, so this shouldn't count against my time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you enlarge this some more, because it's difficult to read the place names. We must find Kosna Luka. I still cannot read it, but I can mark the approximate location [marks]. This is where you enter an area known as Kosna Luka, and this was the last check-point of the ABiH facing Doljani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you may have difficulty discerning the road to Doljani because of the arrow marked here, but it can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of 4D02025 shall be given Exhibit IC01179. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak is on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have maps in the Detention Unit, so tomorrow I can provide a better map which is more easily legible, and I can show that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, but if you take Map IC 1124, which is also in the first binder, you can actually read "Kosta Luka," you can actually see where the location is, and I can confirm that it is where Mr. Petkovic has marked it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have difficulties with my eyesight, so I may have missed the exact location by a couple of hundred metres, but it must be thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel, for this clarification. I believe this was very useful.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could, please, the judge's microphone be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The following document about this topic is 4D1079. It's a report about the situation in the territory of Jablanica and Konjic which, on May 5th, 1993, was sent to the HVO General Staff and signed by the members of the commission, Stanko Maric and Bozo Raguz. Tell us, General, did you have the chance to see the report at the time when it was sent there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. These two persons were with me. They drafted a report for me, although I was with them all the time, and I knew all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A correction of the document reference. It is 4D1079. General, in item 1 of this report we can read that one of the commissions visited the areas of Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina in the presence of General Petkovic and Halilovic. And it goes on to say: "Everything that was requested has been taken care of or resolved." Does this refer to the evacuation of civilians from Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm now done with the topic of the evacuation of Sovici and Doljani. If you have further questions, this is the right time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, regarding the last document, I have a small technical question to ask you. There is mention of Mr. Pusic. Was he with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, Mr. Pusic was in the other group. I had two groups, two teams. I represented the Main Staff. There was Colonel Filipovic, there was Zebic, Sergeant Zebic -- Captain Zebic, Maric and Raguz from the operative zone. And Mr. Pusic belonged to another group led by Dr. Bagaric and the others, and they arrived with 15 ambulances, and they were to be divided into three groups for pulling out the wounded, sick, the fatalities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at this document, I note that Colonel Morales was there. Do you remember his presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Now, you asked about the meeting in the tent. The colonel who was there was Colonel Morales, the commander of SpaBat at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, we can see that yourself, Pasalic, and Halilovic were discussing things, and at one point in time Pasalic said that Mostar was a concentration camp for Muslims. When he was saying that, what was Colonel Morales saying? Did he agree with that, or did he tell Pasalic, Come on, you're exaggerating? As far as you remember, what was his reaction? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Colonel Morales did not react in any way. And if you recall the beginning of that conversation, when General Halilovic asked the UNPROFOR representatives to allow us to communicate amongst ourselves, I'm sure you'll remember that and the beginning of the footage, Mr. Halilovic asked that they let us communicate amongst ourselves. And if they want to listen to our communications, they could do so, so that Colonel Morales didn't meddle in our discussions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wasn't there sometimes a tendency to exaggerate? Here, I note that it says that there are 5.000 people imprisoned in Zenica, and Sefer, i.e., Sefer Halilovic, says that there are 5.000. Are you sure of that? Sefer holds 5.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zenica, there were about 45 per cent incarcerated from two of our brigades, which would be about 1.300 men. We had two brigades in Zenica. However, neither of them were very large in numbers. And according to our information, there were about 1300 people -- members of the HVO in those two brigades who were incarcerated. The largest portion was in Zenica prison. I forget the name of the prison. Anyway, 500 people were there, and others were held in schools and other facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that doesn't add up to 5.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't write this number, "5.000." Either the gentleman didn't understand me when I was talking about the numbers and knew that there were 500 people in the Zenica prison, so all I can assume is that one knot was added there by mistake. So I can put that right straight right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's move on to the next area and see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you think this would be a convenient moment for me asking the question on Sovici and Doljani? Thank you, I see that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I would like to confront you with what I find in paragraphs 76, 77, 78, and following in the indictment, which speaks about detainees, some 70 to 80 military-aged Bosnian Muslims, in the school of Sovici, to which you have already referred, and alleges that at least four people were killed there and others were mistreated. I can imagine what your answer to this is, but I would like to give you the opportunity to state your position on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the school in Sovici, there are about 50 people, and those people were put in that school about two days or three days before we arrived in the area. According to the commander, it was for security reasons, because certain groups were coming into the Sovici and Doljani area, and the only way in which these people could be protected was that. I don't accept that this was a concentration camp or anything else, given the situation that prevailed -- or a camp of any kind, for that matter. People were simply put up there in that way, and they were under security, and nobody could reach them. As far as the fatalities are concerned, what I know about that is that in Sovici it was in combat that about seven people were killed, as far as I remember, and that all of them had the status of members of the 4th Battalion, the 44th Brigade from Jablanica. I don't know of a single civilian being killed in any way. Similarly, I had no report coming in from Sovici and Doljani about any abuse or mistreatment of these people. No report of that kind reached the Main Staff. And there were people, mostly women, that were working around their houses, cultivating the land around their homes, their own backyards. So that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Petkovic, they were detained for security. Could you specify what you mean by saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the commander of the battalion in Sovici, after what had happened on the 21st, quite simply was afraid that some groups would turn up again and take it out on the civilians, so all these people, when they entered Sovici, they didn't have any weapons and they were all left in Sovici. Otherwise, they would have joined up with the group of 85, I think it was, soldiers who were relocated as soldiers who surrendered to the Military Investigative Prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I was not sufficiently precise in my question. The indictment says that these 70 to 90 -- and you say it was 50, and let's see whether we talk about the same people, in the first place. You said that they were detained after the events of the 20-21st April to protect them against attacks by uncontrolled elements. According to the indictment, they were detained on the 17th-18th of April, that is, before these events. Also, it is specified that they were military-aged Bosnian Muslim men. This does not quite fit with the explanation you have given, and perhaps you now want to give another explanation and also clarify, perhaps, why a misunderstanding may have arisen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I understand your question better now. I was wondering whether you had in mind a number of 85 -- the figure of 85 people who, on the 17th and 18th, surrendered. Those were BH Army soldiers, and on the 17th, in the afternoon, they surrendered, and on the 18th, too. And after talking to them and providing transport for them, they were, indeed, transported to the Military Investigative Prison from Sovici. They were transferred to the prison from Sovici. Now, as far as I'm concerned, that is normal military procedure. These were soldiers. They surrendered in proper fashion, surrendered their weapons. A list of those people was compiled, and they had nothing but to surrender and be handed over to the military prison. So that's as far as these 85 people are concerned, and I stand by the fact that on the 18th that is the way they were relocated from Sovici to Ljubuski. They were soldiers of the BH Army, belonging to the 4th Battalion, led by their commander, Mr. Ovnovic, and that is standard procedure. Now, whether somebody was mistreated or not, I wasn't there, Judge Trechsel, so I can't claim either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am not quite convinced that we are talking about the same. But I will leave it at that, and if the Prosecution wants to take this up, I will let them. I just wanted to give you an opportunity to state your view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, could you look at the exact wording of the indictment, and then you'll see that General Petkovic gave you the answer precisely as it is put in the indictment. In paras 76, 77, and 79, they relate to members of the BH Army who were incarcerated between the 17th and 18th of April and who, on the 18th of April, were transferred to Ljubuski, so they were detained then. Now, this group of various detainees has nothing to do with a group of men -- with the group of men who were in the school on the 4th of May, 1993, when the delegation arrived, including General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're testifying now. I'm afraid you're testifying, Ms. Alaburic, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I'm just reading the indictment, that's all I'm doing, and it's quite clear there. And we are discussing Sovici and Doljani precisely for the Trial Chamber's benefit, so it's -- so we do want you to understand and to avoid any misunderstanding. So look at what the rest of the indictment says. It goes on to speak about the burning of houses and people who were put up in Sovici and Doljani, but these others were a group of detainees, and that is an undisputed fact. And on the 18th of April, they were, indeed, transferred to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I read what I found -- what I see in the indictment, and it's paragraph 77: "On 17 to 18 April 1993, the HVO collected and detained approximately 70 to 90 military-aged Bosnian Muslim men at a school in Sovici." It does not say that soldiers of the ABiH who had surrendered were placed there. Perhaps that is what the case was, but it does not say so here. The soldiers of the ABiH are mentioned, I think, in the previous paragraphs, which refers to Bosnian men, I quote, "attempting to defend the villages," which again does not mention, as you have said, members of the ABiH. So I reject your observation that I have not taken -- looked at the indictment, but I do not want to argue this point with you now, nor with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can contribute. General Petkovic, my fellow Judge read out the paragraphs in the indictment, and they were very clear. You have 70 to 90 men, and of military age - I insist on that - and they were detained in that school. When reading this, you immediately think these are not ABiH soldiers. However, at the time there was -- the imminent state of war had been proclaimed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I believe. I believe that there were also documents in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna providing that any person -- any able-bodied man or person was meant or supposed to take part in the war effort. So these, quote/unquote, "civilians" who were defending their village, according to you, as commander of the HVO, as actually a head of staff of the HVO, these people were potentially ABiH soldiers who possibly or desirably should be detained, or watched, or kept under guard, so forth and so on. What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, and Your Honours, these were soldiers of the BH Army, and if we were to look at the indictment, we would only find five BH Army soldiers for the whole war. In this indictment, there are no BH Army soldiers, except Halilovic and Izetbegovic. That is the Prosecution's position. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). After three hours of fighting at the Sovici gates, he withdrew his forces to Sovici proper. And when he saw that he could not put up a resistance, he acted as a true battalion commander and handed over his soldiers, had his soldiers surrender. No unarmed civilians. They were soldiers of the BH Army who, on the evening of the 15th, placed under complete siege Doljani and the battalion of the HVO. They were no civilians. They were soldiers. And throughout the indictment, mention is made of civilians. No commanders are mentioned. There's nobody here in court. That is the tactics of the OTP. I claim that they were all BH Army soldiers, they were all recorded, they all returned their rifles. We know the number of the rifle, et cetera. So they weren't civilians. The 44th Brigade was formed far before that and existed as such. Therefore, they were soldiers of the BH Army who, three hours prior to their surrender, had been fighting at the Sovici gates, and their commander, faced with a situation he could not contend with, surrendered. And they were soldiers of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If they weren't, who was it that we were fighting against, six soldiers of the BH Army throughout? And Halilovic said that there were 24.000 [as interpreted] of them, so is it possible the HVO had soldiers and not the HV Army -- or not the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, in this type of conflict, is it not difficult to make a distinction between civilians and soldiers? And I will follow up. Yesterday, I was looking into a complaint from Amnesty International against the chief of staff of the Canadian forces in Afghanistan, because the Canadian Army would allegedly have detained civilians on the Kandahar Base, and at the moment a legal action has been launched against General Hillier, H-i-l-l-i-e-r. I assume that this Canadian general was able to make a distinction between civilians and military men. But all the same, I was wondering whether it was easy or not to make a distinction between civilians and military men. And I will follow in on that. When the Vranica building was taken, some soldiers from the ABiH had dressed up as civilians. Some witnesses testified on that. So according to you, was it easy to make a distinction between a civilian and a military person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, let me first return to Sovici and Doljani. Over there, there were no difficulties -- rather, there was no problem to tell civilians from soldiers. The commander lined up his soldiers and started to surrender his units. They all wore uniforms, they all had their weapons, and they were registered accordingly. Only -- they were only kept at the school from the 17th through the 18th because it was impossible to conduct an interview with everybody and do everything necessary to take them to detention. They were soldiers of the ABiH, its 44th Brigade commanded by their commander, Mr. Ovnovic. There were no civilians, because that brigade didn't consist of 2.000 civilians, but of 2.000 soldiers. At Vranica and anywhere, if you see somebody in civilian clothes you can say, Well, he's a soldier, or, He's not a soldier. But if you find -- or, He has an adequate ID on him, then he's a soldier. And if he's able to give pertinent information about his unit, he's also a soldier. And the very fact of their leaving Vranica and changing clothes clearly shows that they were soldiers rather than civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to dispel any misunderstanding possible, I was not taking any issue with that. But what you are saying shows that these persons were not detained so that they be protected from any further individuals that would come and revenge the death of Cikota, I think was his name, but they were rather detained because they were considered a danger. And that, I think, is also what is the meaning in the indictment, so this point is clarified, and I would not like to be understood as having taken a position on the issue of who is a military and who is not. That was not the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said immediately that there had been a misunderstanding. When you asked your question, I thought you meant the persons I found there. But when you mentioned the dates of the 17th and the 18th, it became clear to me who exactly you meant. Initially, I meant the other group that had stayed at Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a remark to the transcript before we go too far, and there might be a question about it. At page 37, line 7, it reads that General Petkovic said that General Halilovic said that they were 240.000 in all, whereas the transcript reads "24.000." I believe the general can confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 240.000, that's what he states in his book, and he also said to me, person to person, how many soldiers they had carrying arms, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have our first break. We'll have a 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we continue, I would like to say the following: The topic raised by Judge Trechsel is very important, and it's a comprehensive topic, and we will deal with it in the redirect. I would like to voice the concern of the Petkovic Defence and some other colleagues to whom I spoke during the break, and it has to do with our understanding of Judge Trechsel's comment. We understood that comment to mean that some claims in the indictment are considered true unless proven otherwise, and that that was the reason why the Petkovic Defence's argument that these were two separate groups of men held at the Sovici school were not believed, only for the reason that this differed from the statements in the indictment. We would like to remind of the fact that it is up to the OTP to prove the claims in the indictment and that these are to be considered -- are not to be considered true unless proven so. So we would like to avoid any such misunderstanding in the future, and that is why we will deal with this topic in depth in the redirect. I believe that we will be able to clarify all dilemmas and that the state of affairs was, indeed, as described by General Petkovic rather than as put forward in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I think your suspicion is nonsense. This is a strong word, but that's really how I feel. And I would like you to look at page 38, line 25. The question I put was to give an opportunity to state a view, and that is all, and there is most definitely no presumption of anything being true or not. It is really helpful assistance to the Defence, in fact. That is what it is intended to be, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to add one more sentence. If my understanding and that of my colleagues, who understood your comment to mean the same as I did, if that understanding is wrong, I wish to apologise. I appreciate your efforts to state your opinion clearly, whether any Defence likes it or not, and we consider it our duty to be just as frank as you are. And we apologise if anything we say may cause lack of understanding on any part. We would like to continue our co-operation in the spirit of good understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the accused. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start from the beginning again. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreters can hear you. We can no longer hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not a lawyer, but I believe that I've learned something in these four years. As far as I know, in the redirect only such issues can be dealt with if any Defence or the Prosecutor or the Judges raised that issue before. How can a Defence counsel know in advance that anybody will, indeed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is switched off. The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But saying things out openly, without anybody reacting except me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can my Defence be deprived of the right to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, there is a problem with the microphone, so perhaps you could use another microphone. There seems to be a problem with the one just in front of you. Can you perhaps speak in the mike in front of Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence counsel said several times today that she wouldn't deal with some issues in the examination-in-chief, but would instead deal with them in the redirect. My question is: How does counsel know that anybody from the OTP or from the Defence teams or any Judge will raise the issue to give her the right to deal with that in the redirect? Secondly, I noticed some time ago that crucial issues are left for the redirect to prevent the Defence teams from dealing with some issues that worried them in the cross-examination. It is a sad fact that I, as an accused person, have to react to that, because there are others who should do that in my stead, because I'm not a lawyer. And I needn't be right, but I believe that I am on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may answer Mr. Coric. I have said several times in this courtroom that 20 to 25 per cent of the time earmarked for direct examination is used by the questions of the Judges. This morning, I said that because of the shortage of time, I would not like to continue that way. Instead, the Judges' questions are -- that I will deal with such matters in the redirect. So this referred exclusively to issues raised by the questions of the Judges. My last mention of the redirect was prompted by the question asked by Judge Trechsel about item 76 through 79 of the indictment. I believe the accused remembers that much evidence was submitted with regard to that, and that it is clear to the Judges what has been proven with regard to that or not. At no time did it enter my mind to deal in the redirect with any topic that wasn't raised by the questions of the Judges or anybody else in the courtroom. However, if such topics as haven't been covered in the examination-in-chief, in the cross-examination, I preserve the right to deal with that in the redirect. I believe that now Mr. Coric understands my position better. It was never my intention to do anything in the redirect that is not provided for by the Rules of this Tribunal, and the attorney of Mr. Coric is a very good lawyer, and she certainly wouldn't allow any such thing to happen. And, besides, the Judges know the Rules very well, too, and wouldn't allow that to happen either.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As a discussion has started that may be premature, but as we have it on our hands now, I would like to support Mr. Coric's words, but it is too early because we will have to wait to see whether, in the redirect, issues will be raised that have not been dealt -- haven't been dealt with before. I understand Ms. Alaburic's problems with the allotted time, but irrespective of that, the topics raised by the Judges during the examination-in-chief, that is, the questions they ask, are dealt with in the examination-in-chief. They cannot be left for the redirect. And it's another matter if, during the cross-examination, the Judges ask questions about issues that were not dealt with in the examination-in-chief. At that time, the Defence team who had the examination-in-chief has the right to object or, rather, to take up the issue itself. Now, at this time we, of course, cannot know what Ms. Alaburic wants to deal with in the redirect. We may be faced with new information about which everybody here may wish to cross-examine once more. It is clear that the redirect can only refer to the cross-examination and the topics dealt with there. I'm very sorry that my colleague has problems with time, but everybody else has such -- the same problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me just one more sentence about this. The right of any Defence team for a redirect after the Judge's question was something that was decided upon in this courtroom before. We submitted a motion about that, and there is a relevant decision of the Trial Chamber. I believe that we must simply adhere to the decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will proceed. I wanted to say something, because I want it to be in the transcript. When I personally ask a question, but I believe that it's the same for my colleagues -- when a Judge asks a question, the question has to be fully rounded, and the witness has to answer fully to the question, which means that there is no need for a follow-up question or any additional question. If a need arises, it would mean that the Judge did not put the question properly, either because he did not understand the problem or he has a few things that are missing in his documentation. But usually a Judge who understands the problem well, a Judge who is listening, who has the documents before him, when such a Judge asks a question, the witness should answer fully to the question and there should not be any follow-up question, because the witness has said what he had to say. And this is why sometimes I'm surprised that there are some follow-up questions. But, of course, I can make a mistake, like everybody else, but be aware that when I ask a question, I have carefully thought of the question before. It doesn't come off the cuff, and it is part of all the evidence that we have heard until now, 50.000 pages of transcript as well as 10.000 exhibits. So all my questions are asked through those filters, so to say. But, of course, a counsel may feel that the answer from the witness is not sufficient and, therefore, ask for follow-up questions, but usually I have to say I am surprised that follow-up questions are asked. I find that rather strange. For instance, when I asked questions to General Petkovic on the investigation made by the military prosecutor, he answered, and I didn't feel that any follow-up question needed to be asked, because what was important was to know that an investigation had been carried out. But at the same time, I can also make mistakes. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we continue, I'd like to tell you that we have handed over a document, information about Petkovic's movements for 1993, principally, so that you can look at the most important months, that is to say, April, May, and June 1993. You can see where General Petkovic was from one day to the next. 2027 -- 4D2027 is the document number, and you can all use it, and we might be using it during further examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, if the conflict was a broader one and a more lasting one between the HVO and BH Army, and if it began in mid-April 1993, tell us, please, how long did the conflict between the two armies actually last?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict between these two armies lasted until about the beginning of May. There was a brief lull, and then it continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak -- or, rather, General Petkovic, in the question put by Ms. Alaburic there is a problem. She says if the conflict started around mid-April, if it began in mid-April, but I understood that the ABiH had launched an attack in January. So I'm rather lost here. Does that mean that the HVO-ABiH conflict happened in mid-April and nothing happened in January? This is where I am at a loss, and perhaps you can shed some light by answering very precisely to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army occurred in January 1993, and it was definitely completed on the 29th of February, 1993. Those are the dates we counted as -- we count as being the period. And General Halilovic and I undertook steps in the area, Busovaca and so on, in Central Bosnia to bring about an end, and then there was for a time a lull when the situation was calm, until the 23rd of March, 1993, when the conflict began in the Konjic municipality with the attack by the BH Army on the HVO. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Petkovic. There was no 29th of February in 1993. You want to correct that date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour. Well, the last day. Well, the conflict lasted until the 27th -- 26th, 27th. You're quite right. As I said, in March, the 23rd of March, in fact, 1993, we have a situation in Konjic whereby the BH Army launched an attack against the HVO. And on the 25th, in my opinion, we managed to contain the conflict and left teams to supervise -- to monitor the conflict which, from one day to the next, well, it changed in intensity, weaker or stronger. But, anyway, we considered that we had it under control right up until the 13th of April, 1993, when I considered that the conflict took on greater scope; in Konjic municipality, taking on Jablanica. And, as such, it reached full intensity in that area until the 10th of July. At the same time, the conflict spilled over in April to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, General Petkovic gave us some dates, and I believe these are important dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Those are all dates that we mentioned yesterday when we discussed the conflicts in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next area, General, is: How were these conflicts stopped in April?
