utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that the French language, like the B/C/S, is a very precise language, and when I said General Petkovic gave us dates that were important, I'm not saying that I believe that they are important; this is what General Petkovic believes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood it, Your Honour, because these are precisely dates that we mentioned in our opening statement as being the most important ones for an understanding of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least with respect to the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's see how these conflicts were stopped in April. Ahmici occurred on the 16th of April. In Sovici and Doljani, the fighting was on the 17th of April, 1993. And now let's look at the first document dealing with this area. 2D89 is the number. This is an agreement between Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, dated the 18th of April, 1993, on a cessation to all conflicts and the need to resolve all misunderstandings through political means, to free prisoners, release prisoners, and to determine the responsibility of individuals and units for the start of the confrontations. Now, tell me, General, did you know of this agreement when it was reached?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who informed you about the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed about this agreement by Mr. Boban, personally, and he said that on the 18th a delegation with Mr. Thebault, General Pellnas and so on, Mr. Ganic -- yes, and Mr. Ganic, was supposed to leave and that General Morillon would bring to Mostar Mr. Halilovic too, and that linked to this agreement we would continue to do everything to calm the situation down in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, on that day, if we look at this breakdown of your movements - it is 4D2027, the document - for the 18th of April, your meeting in Mostar is mentioned, organised by the European Observers. Tell us, please, was the meeting actually held in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this meeting was that we should, with the help of the international community, UNPROFOR, the Military Observers and Monitoring Mission, that I and General Halilovic should have a meeting and issue joint orders and move towards the actual areas where the conflicts were taking place and to put them under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, P1959, General, please, which is an order of yours dated the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put an ancillary question, but which has to do with this document. This is a document signed by Izetbegovic and Boban. According to the Prosecution's case, as you know, Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Community, and the HVO are illegal entities, and there is a decision by the Constitutional Court. I have here a document where the president of the Presidency has signed a document together with Mr. Mate Boban, which is, at first glance, a person that would be, quote/unquote, "illegal." So when you were negotiating in the international negotiations in Geneva, you told us yesterday that you actually went up in the plane with Mr. Izetbegovic to go to Geneva. We weren't there, we Judges were not there, so we don't know what was said or what happened, but we are all -- we all know that international negotiations were going on. Among the four Judges, two of them were ambassadors and the two others also attended these kind of international meetings. So you have here on the Bench Judges who actually know what international negotiations are all about. And this is where you can contribute: In the discussions that you were having -- in the informal discussions you were having with all those involved in these kind of negotiations, well, how was Mr. Boban perceived; as an intruder, as someone who was illegal, or as someone worthy of respect, whose word was taken into account to the extent that he could actually sign an important document, et cetera? So what image did Mr. Mate Boban convey among all the others that you were with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me answer your first question first. The Constitutional Court never annulled the military part of the Croatian Defence Council. The military part of the Croatian Defence Council entered within the composition of the BH Army. What the Constitution did was to annul the Decree on the Armed Forces, which is something quite different. Furthermore, at the negotiations in Geneva, we had the representatives of the three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mate Boban was viewed as the elected representative of the Croatian people, completely legally, just like the representative of the Serbian people, Mr. Karadzic; and the Muslim Bosniak people, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. And in the talks and the negotiations, they enjoyed the same status and were treated the same way, and their positions and views were respected and taken on board. Now, as far as the Geneva negotiations are concerned, Mr. Boban, I would say, was favourable to the negotiators' efforts, because he recognised Mr. Owen's plan, the Vance-Owen Plan, first among the three, and as such, placed his signature on the plan and, thus, encouraged them to continue the negotiations with the other two representatives or the representatives of the other two nations from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Mate Boban enjoyed a status of equality with everybody else. Mate Boban, even outside Geneva, had quite a lot of contacts with the representatives of the international community, co-chairmen, with meetings in Zagreb and so on, so Mate Boban was accepted as a completely legal representative of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the next document is P1959, and it is your order also dated the 18th of April, 1993, on a cessation of hostilities between the BH Army and the HVO. And as it says in the introduction, you issued this order on the basis of the conclusions reached in talks between Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic and their agreement. So tell us, General, did you actually sign this order, yourself, or was it signed for you by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order followed on from the agreement, and the signature is that of Mr. Zeljko Arkan [as interpreted], and the reason is very simple. The order was finished but hadn't been typed out yet, and I had to hurry to the Mostar Hospital because Mr. Thebault was waiting there, as well as General Pellnas and the delegation which arrived. So to be encoded, it had to have a signature, and then Mr. Akrap signed for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, in point 5 we see that you are ordering the establishment and contacts with the BH Army command, and you're asking them to implement the same order. Tell us, please, General, as far as personal contacts are concerned between the BH Army and HVO, did you consider them to be important for the establishment of a cease-fire and for maintaining law and order and resolving the dispute and conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I did, yes, because without mutual personal contact between commanders on the ground, it was impossible to implement any order or document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's go on to the next document, which is P2036, and it is once again one of your orders on measures to deal with self-will and arbitrary behaviour on behalf of individuals and groups, and you sent it to all the zones on the 22nd of April, 1993. And you say here, and I'll summarise, that the most extreme individuals and groups who are out of control and who are destroying civilian facilities and so on and so forth, they must be stopped by all means, including the use of force. Now, tell us, please, General, was this just your own personal position, or was that the position taken by the leadership of Herceg-Bosna as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a joint position taken that we should put a stop to this kind of behaviour on the part of individuals and groups, working off their own bat. Otherwise, the document came into being two days after I arrived in Central Bosnia and returned to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us your opinion, General. Did HVO commanders, to the best of your knowledge, ever have the intention to achieve military, political, or other goals by burning buildings, driving civilians out of their homes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document, P2038. It's a demand of yours, dated the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I'm sorry again to interrupt you, but I really feel that your question was rather, in a way, a leading one, because I believe that nobody would think that the answer should be other than, Yes. So, therefore, I think that in the future you may have a look at it, how to put your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate your opinion that this was a leading question, but I respectfully disagree because this is one of the allegations in the indictment. It is very important for us to know the position of the accused on that issue. He may have answered that he knew some commanders who, in their area of responsibility, instigated or tolerated or tried to achieve some objectives by illegitimate means.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if you have anything to add, we can do this later, but we can also do it while discussing the following document, P2036. Tell us, General, about the position of the commanders of the HVO and the supreme commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the interpreters are breathless. You're going too fast. Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours. To start with, let me correct the document reference. P2038.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a demand you made, General, which was sent to the operative zones about conduct towards civilians and prisoners. Can you tell us the position of the supreme commander of the HVO and lower-level commanders about how the military is supposed to treat civilians and prisoners of war, respectively? Very briefly, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All levels, from the supreme commander downward, demanded that the civilian population be respected, that they should not be involved in the combat activities, and this was demanded of all commands at all levels. Likewise, arrested soldiers and detained civilians must be provided adequate protection. The ICRC must be granted access -- and not only granted access, but they must also be informed of the presence of such persons at any location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The following document, General, is 4D1082. This is a demand of yours, sent to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and the Herceg Stjepan Brigade at Konjic. You request information about the events in these areas, and you are mentioning that this information is intended for Mate Boban. Is this your document, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is this the document we spoke about yesterday and based on which you received information from the ground, including Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the very document we spoke about yesterday, and it was drafted after my talks with Mr. Boban and his request for additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the two following documents. 4D576, this is a letter dated October 13th, 1993, which Tihomir Blaskic sent to Mate Boban, and in this letter he speaks about assignments he received in the office of the supreme commander on the 28th of September, 1993. Tell us, General, what does this document tell us about the communication between the commander-in-chief and Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it says that the supreme commander received Colonel Blaskic personally, and he spoke to him for four hours without requesting the presence of anybody from the Main Staff. So they spoke in private for all these four hours, and they never informed anybody of the contents of their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the Main Staff, although you weren't chief of Main Staff at the time, did you know that the supreme commander had direct communication with individual military commanders, bypassing the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We knew that Mr. Boban had this weakness of granting private conversations to anybody upon their request, ignoring the fact that the presence of someone from the Main Staff was actually required, or somebody from the zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The transcript reads "private conversation." Tell us, based on this letter, is this a conversation about private matters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't about private matters. It's an official conversation between the supreme commander and Colonel Blaskic, so they discussed matters of interest to the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item 3 of this letter reads: "The Ahmici case will be finished according to the instructions given. The activity is underway, but most of the task has been carried out." The following document follows up directly, so let's take a look at it. It's document 4D575. On the 6th of December, 1993, Tihomir Blaskic reports to Mate Boban directly about the carrying out of the assignments received in the supreme commander's office, and he says: "The Ahmici case has been completed according to our instructions ..." Tell us, how do you understand these two letters, written by Tihomir Blaskic, from today's vantage point?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here's how I understand this to mean: That the commander-in-chief personally got involved in the investigation about Ahmici. And all subsequent steps taken by Tihomir Blaskic were based on an agreement reached between these two persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now go briefly into your activities in the month of April after signing the cease-fire agreement. In document 4D2027, it is recorded that on the 20th of April, you were in Zenica, and talked to Halilovic in the presence of representatives of the international community. On the following day, on the 21st of April, you were in Vitez also with Halilovic, in the presence of Ambassador Thebault. Then, on the 24th and 25th of April, you were in Zagreb at a meeting of the Croatian and Muslim delegations with the co-chairman for the former Yugoslavia. There, an agreement was reached which we have seen zillions of times here in this courtroom. After Zagreb, on the 28th, you were in Zenica with Halilovic again. On the same day, you also visited Jablanica. On the following day, the 29th of April, you were in Vitez and Zenica, again with Halilovic and the representatives of the international community. On the 30th of April, you were in Zenica with Halilovic again, and thus we reach May. Then there's a brief interval during which you didn't meet Halilovic, but you met him again on the 4th of May in Jablanica. We spoke a lot about that today and yesterday. Then on the 5th of May, again. From these documents -- or, rather, it follows from this information that roughly from the 18th of April, 1993, until the 5th of May, you continuously, almost daily except for a brief interval around the 1st of May, had meetings with Halilovic and visited forces on the ground. Was it really like that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and it had to do with the initial agreement between Boban and Izetbegovic of the 17th and the Zagreb agreement of the 25th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will now deal with the issue of May 1993 in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you returned from the area of Jablanica, where you were with Halilovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier, you mentioned Ahmici. Ahmici is mentioned in the pre-trial brief, but is not blamed on the accused. But it was mentioned to explain that the HVO had been launching a general offensive, according to the Prosecution's case, anyway. Now, I would like to know the following, General Petkovic: Within international negotiations, the negotiations you attended, was Ahmici mentioned often, this issue of Ahmici, or was it just a very unfortunate event, a dramatic event, but that was sort of not really mentioned by those who were involved in the international negotiations; otherwise, they would have had to also deal with Trusina and other municipalities? So as far as you remember, was Ahmici a central issue that led to many consequences, or was it just not taken into account, at least not in all of its aspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the latter is the case, and I'll try to explain. On the 20th, we were in Zenica and talked all afternoon. You saw the agreements. No one of the ABiH representatives mentioned Ahmici at all. Nobody from the international community did either. On the following day, the 21st, Halilovic and I went to at least 10 locations to separate forces. Never once did ABiH personnel raise the issue of Ahmici, nor did they suggest that we go there. Likewise, the talks that we had at the British Battalion was an occasion where nobody ever mentioned Ahmici. We spoke about the area of Central Bosnia, about all events of the time, but nobody mentioned Ahmici. On the 24th and 25th, during the talks in Zagreb, nobody made specific mention of Ahmici. All talks were general, at the general level, things that happened in Central Bosnia and Western Herzegovina. That's what our conversations were like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The first weekend after you returned from your meetings with Halilovic, what did you do on that weekend?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halilovic and I departed in Jablanica in the afternoon of the 5th, because he said to me that he had to go to Sarajevo, he had some important business there, and we agreed to meet on the next Monday. I believe that was the 10th. I used the time available to me to go home to see my family in Split on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which month is that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That Friday, which date was that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the 7th, the 7th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That weekend, in the Main Staff, as far as you know, was it a regular weekend, or were there any differences when you compare it to the previous weekends?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would call it a more relaxed weekend, because while I was at those meetings from the 18th I required the presence of five to six people in the Main Staff. Once I returned, I said, Well, let's have three people, which was the minimum number of officers on duty required, and everybody else was allowed to go home because they had been away from their families for a long time, so that only three persons stayed there who were on duty on the 8th and 9th. And you see that Mr. Peric was the highest-ranking duty officer, but he was -- he wasn't a chief or a commander. He was merely an officer in charge of communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that you returned to Mostar on the 9th of May, in the early afternoon hours, between 1.00 and 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer to this question, I have a technical question which is not going to hamper, I hope, Ms. Alaburic's questions. You left for Split on the 7th of May. The 7th of May is a Friday, because we know that the 9th of May is a Sunday. So you are leaving for Split. Split, unless I'm mistaken, is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, Split is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you are setting off for Croatia, what is the means of communication that you have available with your staff? Is it a satellite telephone, is it your land line, was it means from the Croatian Army? How can you stay in touch with your Main Staff if anything happens? What was a technical way or means of communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had a standard telephone and my telephone number while I lived in Split temporarily, and my family lived there. And I left the number with the duty officers, where I was supposed to leave it. And, secondly, I had - what was it called? - a Benefon, or, anyway, a mobile phone which was built into the car, because it was a box that weighed one kilo, so you couldn't carry it around with you. It was built into the car. And the car I used -- well, I used a heavy-duty vehicle, and I also used a passenger vehicle. So if it was in the heavy-duty vehicle and I wasn't riding in that, then they couldn't establish a mobile telephone connection with me in any way. So that was the only possible communication. That was the only way they could reach me or that I could reach the Main Staff. There were no other ways of communicating, especially not satellite communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering if you had a driver in this vehicle where you had this Benefon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have a driver. And if this off-road vehicle needed to be driven, then the driver would drive it, and he would also drive the passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If, on Sunday, the 9th of February [as interpreted], your wife asks you to buy a kilo of tomatoes at the market-place which is a kilometre away from your home, you go and set off to buy those tomatoes on foot, how can we get hold of you if there are no more means of communications between you and the Main Staff? How is that possible, given that you are chief of staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the technical feasibility was such had there been a mobile phone at the time, I would have carried it 'round with me all the time. But to go to a shop and to come back doesn't take too much time, so it would only require 15 minutes or half an hour. And, of course, there's a team of people. There are lower-level commands who can deal with the problems and situations in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we all understood that at line 17 you meant May and not February. You talked about the 9th of. In the English interpretation, we got "February," anyway, and I'm sure Your Honour was talking about May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are fully right, Mr. Stewart. I didn't notice, but indeed I meant the 9th of May. Very well. So you're saying that the only means of communication was your land line at home or this Benefon on board this vehicle. But if there was any problem, there would be people in a position to answer whatever request or meet any needs. So I take note of what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Well, the three men in the command could react. The commander of the operative zone is closer to his operative zone than I was, and it's his duty to react at any given point in time. So there are a whole series of people who have the duty to react under certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us -- General, you returned to Mostar in the early afternoon. Did you return alone or were you with someone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and Mr. Stojic returned together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And, tell us, did you return in a vehicle of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Stojic. He drove the vehicle that he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us why you and Mr. Stojic happened to be in the same car that day.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were on our way to Tomislavgrad and the operative zone, according to an agreement, to visit Siljeg. And upon receiving information stating that something was happening in Mostar, we did an about-turn and drove back to Mostar, and arrived between 1.00 and 1.30; certainly after 1.00, but not long afterwards. And each of us went to take up his post upon arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, during that day, the 9th of May, did you meet Mr. Stojic again at any time that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Stojic, at around 5.00, called and that he left Mostar. I think it was 'round about 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, when you reached the Main Staff, what did they tell you? What was it that was happening in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the Main Staff, I called some of the people I needed to see, and the first thing I asked them was -- because when I entered the headquarters, I heard some shooting at a distance of some 500 metres up at the confrontation line between the BH Army and the HVO, so the first thing I wanted to know from them was whether they knew where we were and where the BH Army was in town, and the lines in town, and they tried to provide me with the right answer, to the best of their knowledge. And I also asked them to find Mr. Lasic for me, that he should report to me at headquarters. And I think that some 35 minutes later, Mr. Lasic arrived at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you try to contact somebody in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had the telephone numbers -- well, I had two or three telephones used by the members of the 4th Corps and the 41st Brigade, and I gave the communications people instructions to try and contact somebody from the 41st Brigade or 4th Corps because I said I'd like to speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, why did you wish to contact the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conflict had to be stopped, and you can't have one side stopping a conflict, especially when there's fighting in a built-up area. You could do so perhaps in a mountainous area, and then you say, Well, I'll stop shooting and see what happens. But when you're in town, it's very difficult to do that. So to put a stop to the conflict, the other side -- the other party to the conflict must be of the same mind and receive orders to stop the conflict, and then try to implement this on the ground through the various levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you finally manage to reach someone from the 4th BH Army Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't reach anybody, but we did manage to ring two telephone numbers. One was from South Camp, and the other was from Konak [phoen] or whatever the name was. But when they heard that it was the HVO calling, they cut the line, so I was not -- and I was not able to establish communication with anybody from the 4th Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, when the commander of the operative zone, Mr. Lasic, arrived at headquarters, and you said that this was towards 2.00 in the afternoon, what did he tell you? What was going on in Mostar, according to him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I asked him questions. I asked him what I was most interested in, and that was to see what our positions were in town. And Mr. Lasic told me that at 2.00 the positions were the same as they were at the start along the Bulevar and the other streets, that at 2.00 p.m. the situation was the same as it was at the beginning, but that there were certain skirmishes of the BH Army towards the Rondo and some other streets leading to that part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. When you speak about incidents created by the BH Army, if we look at the separation line in April 1993, were these incidents to the west of the separation line or to the east of it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the west, to the western part of town. So they crossed the separation line at several points and entrenched in the western parts, and then there was fighting there to try and regain the initial positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did Commander Lasic tell you which units were involved in the fighting against the BH Army in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him that. I asked him what forces he had at his disposal and whether he had sufficient men to hold the line, and he went on to enumerate the forces he had, the parts of the unit, beginning with parts of the 2nd Brigade, which was deployed in a smaller part of town, then the 3rd Brigade, which was from Hum towards town, and then there was the Convicts Battalion, part of the Bruno Busic Brigade, part of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did he mention the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Part of the civilian police, too, was deployed, but that was a small group of the civilian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did any of these units take part at your request? Was it deployed at your request or pursuant to your orders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them could have been deployed on the basis of any of my orders. All those units had already been in combat for a period of eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But, General, you could have used a telephone, for example, or you might have issued an order earlier on, so it's not only important where you were on that morning of the 9th of May, but what you were doing on previous days, in general terms. So tell us whether you perhaps issued an order previously or made a request for the engagement of these or any other units for fighting and combat in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no orders issued, nor was there any need for that, one, two, or three days beforehand, to issue any orders linked to the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, in this courtroom we have seen a number of orders from Miljenko Lasic on the deployment and engagement of additional units because of the situation in Mostar, so tell us now, please, what your understanding of the situation is, the situation at that time. Were these military units engaged for combat because of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively because of the action of the BH Army units and the need for part of the units to be rotated after the urban fighting, and that's why he tried to write orders to bring in other units, reinforcements. However, the writing of orders is one thing, and the arrival of units is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, at that point in time did Lasic have information about the number of casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the report about the number of casualties arrived -- well, no, he didn't know at the time. He didn't have the exact figures at the time. I think that he thought that one or two HVO members had been killed and that there were several others wounded. But towards evening, a report arrived from Lasic, and the figures there were six fatalities and, I think, seventeen wounded, if that incorporated all the units, but that's what it said in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the Judges have already asked you about the evacuation of civilians from this operation zone in Mostar, and I have one additional question on that subject. When did you learn about the ethnic composition of the people who were evacuated and put up at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was on the 12th, in the afternoon, after the signing of an agreement in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, are we talking about May; is that still May?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 12th of May, after the agreement had been signed calling for the release of these individuals. And through the operative zone from Medjugorje I called up to have information collected about the people who were at Heliodrom, and that's when I learnt what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And, tell us, was the vast majority of these people Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. However, I'd like to add here that along with the fighting, which started in Mostar, Lasic was confronted with another problem, and that was the need to take in Croats from East Mostar. A part of them were transported across Tito's Bridge, I think was the name of the bridge, and the other section -- the other Croats expelled from East Mostar were moving towards the Buna, and a small group set out from something called the Aviator's Bridge by the Heliodrom, in that same direction, so that he had a problem. He had the problem of evacuating both those from the west bank, who were right by the lines of combat, and also those who were in the area from North Camp, Zalik, towards the east. And I think that area was called Dvojnica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with the supreme commander that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the supreme commander have any information about the events in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he had communicated with - what was his name? - the president of the HVO of Mostar, Mr. Topic, and tried to elicit information from him. Having talked to Lasic, I called him up and relayed the information I received from Lasic to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you pass on to the supreme commander your opinion that immediate contact must be established with the Muslim side and agree on a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I said to him that I thought we had to do that, and he gave me support. He even asked me whether I had tried to reach Halilovic, and I replied in the affirmative. Halilovic and I, on the 28th of April, had exchanged views, because I had learned his satellite phone number by the time, but I didn't reach him. I suppose that he was somewhere in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Boban establish contact with anyone on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban called me up at 7.00 p.m. to come to Grude as soon as possible, if possible, if the fighting had waned, and he expected a conversation with Mr. Izetbegovic. I believe that it was Mr. Tudjman's office that acted as an intermediary on that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did you say that Boban called you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1900 hours, and I really left for Grude at that time to see him. In the meantime, he had spoken to Mr. Izetbegovic and agreed that on the following day they would consider an order that both of them would issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at the first document in this set, and that is 3D1001. This is a report by Miljenko Lasic, dated the 9th of May, 1993, and it describes the situation at 2000 hours. Is this the report you meant when you mentioned the number of wounded and killed persons?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the last report that came in on that day, and it stated the number of killed and injured persons. One civilian had been killed, and four were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the lower left-hand corner, the list to whom this was delivered. There is a bullet point 2 reads "Grude" and a fax number. Do you know whose fax number that is?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the fax number of Mr. Boban at Grude, because Mr. Boban wanted reports from the operative zone to be sent to him directly, without need to be edited before it reaches him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, did Miljenko Lasic inform Mate Boban, that is, the commander-in-chief of the HVO, directly in the course of that day and on subsequent day concerning the conflicts in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first report, but on the following day there was another, and another report on the 11th, and that's how it continues. But on the 10th -- but from the 10th, in the afternoon hours, I was no longer present in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After the meeting with the commander-in-chief at Grude, in the evening hours of the 9th of May, did you return to Mostar that evening or that night?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I stayed at Grude, and I returned in the morning hours, and at 7.00 a.m. I was in Mostar. I stayed until 9.00, 9:00 a.m. That is, I arrived at 7.00 a.m. on the 10th, and I returned at 9.00, because between 10.00 and 11.00, a communication between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban was scheduled concerning the order -- the cease-fire order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stay on this document, 3D1001. You said that it was a report made at 2000 hours by Mr. Lasic on the situation, and so I looked at this report. It says that the situation in Mostar is very difficult. We see that some people are killed, others are wounded, but I do not see in this report anything about a threat from the ABiH, which would take up positions held by the HVO. There is only mention on the fortification of the Bulevar. So when one reads this document, one could have -- I'm using the conditional tense here. I do not have any opinion. My opinion will be made up after deliberations, and that will happen several months from now. So I'm just looking at the various streams of information and thinking here. So when I go through this document, I do not have the feeling that there is a large-scale offensive from the one side or the other. And if there was an HVO offensive targeting the ABiH, I would not understand why, in paragraph 2, we talk about the Serbs, because the main side would be HVO and ABiH, and the Serbs would be in secondary position. But in this report at 2000 hours, we are talking about the Serbs, and this is what I find puzzling, because I have a feeling that there is a general report on a typical situation on the 9th of May, there is some fighting, and it is quite a difficult situation because there are some killed and wounded, but at the same time it doesn't seem that it is very serious. So according to you, what does this report mean, in the military term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already said that in the afternoon hours the situation was calming and that the warring parties were at their -- at the positions from which they had set out, and this is a chronology of events until 2000 hours. Here you can also find certain locations, such as crossing the Rondo, which is a part of Mostar which is to the west of that line, then the area of Celovina. That's a part of town in Mostar, too. Then the Partisan Cinema, then the Ricina Street, the former Santiceva, et cetera, the other locations. And then it reads that the attack at Hum was prevented. So there were some attacks, but they couldn't really jeopardise the western part of Mostar. They were really attempts to enter our territory further, but they didn't come -- they didn't come far. Then when you read the location -- the list of locations, the Ruza Hotel, the Brankovac, et cetera, if we had a map, I could show you the area around the central part. And there was, let's call it, the separation line which was established in April, the Bulevar, the Santiceva Street, and, I believe, Tito's Bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, there's something that I'm quite concerned with for almost four years, ever since we started this trial. It's the capture of the Vranica building. If this building was captured as alleged in the indictment and the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, i.e., within an offensive of the HVO, well, when looking at the problem we've seen videos of the building, we've seen blueprints, maps. I'm really wondering whether this is the correct thing to do, militarily-wise. On May 7th and 8th, everything is quiet, obviously; some are even absent; General Praljak wasn't even there; Mr. Prlic was somewhere else; you're in Split; and so forth and so on. Still, I wonder the following: If this building must absolutely be captured, can it be captured at night with specialists? You know, you had a number of these specialists in store, and when everybody's sleeping, have a targeted attack, a blitz attack, very fast, very professional, and that way you capture the building of the BH Army without shedding blood, or hardly without any fighting. So militarily-wise, was it absolutely impossible to capture the HQ of the BH Army within a blitz commando action at night, without having to unleash all these troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't the HVO's intention then to take the ABiH Command and say, Mission accomplished. That wasn't our assignment. Based on how it was presented to me, it all started with the intention to take the northern camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I follow you, General, I follow you, but let's assume one thing. Let's assume that the HVO did intend to do so. Let's assume that the HVO had the intention of capturing the HQ of the BH Army, I would like to know whether technically you could have done this with a blitz attack, a commando attack, given the fact that there were only a few soldiers. I'm sure at 3.00 in the morning, more than half of them would be sleeping, and maybe one would be reading a newspaper, and that's it. Technically, was it possible to do it that way, given the layout of all this and given that the HQ was in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if there had been considerations to take that building, well, that would have been an option, but there were no considerations to take the building in the night between the 8th and the 9th and resolve the problem of that building in Western Mostar, because, finally, it wasn't really a problem for us. But given the overall situation and considering all events, it was a military problem because of the forces that were coming across the Bulevar. And based on the information I had, this building was defended by some 30-odd soldiers in the lower parts of the building, because that building was -- that part was dug in the ground, and there were snipers at the upper storeys, so that the HVO couldn't access the building. The HVO was removed from the building, trying to shoot at the windows and other openings from which they were firing, and they only surrendered once they had run out of ammunition. If they had had more ammunition, the fighting would have been longer because the entire Vranica building was not being attacked. It was the place where the corps command and the command of the 41st Brigade was. They defended it with some 30-odd soldiers in the basement and on the upper storeys, and there were snipers at the top of that building and surrounding buildings, so it was impossible to access the building; only when we overheard their radio communication that they were running out of ammunition and requesting reinforcements. So there was fighting from a distance. The HVO couldn't access the building to say, Try and throw a hand-grenade inside, or perhaps a tear gas grenade. The HVO returned fire at positions from which they were being shot at - balconies, basements, what have you - because we couldn't get near.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time for our break, it's a quarter to 6.00, so we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a technical matter. We have printed out all the documents, Judge Antonetti, that you prepared for General Petkovic's examination, so I'd now like to hand over the documents or, rather, later on, because I think it will be useful for the general to read through the documents and to be able to have his answers ready to your questions, not to have to waste time on reading the documents. So if you agree, I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned, I have my own binder with all the documents, but you can give your client the list with the documents. I'm sure he has them all, also, and he's had them for some time. But it's true that it would be simpler and will save time. These are all documents that have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take it, then, that I have permission to hand this binder to the general. Thank you. And as I was criticised during the break by our interpreters, I'd like to use this opportunity, in open session, to apologise to the interpreters for speaking so quickly, and also, General, because we don't seem to be making a pause between question and answer. So let's try and do that now and take into account our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Anyway, General, we were discussing the 10th of May, and you said that at 10.00 you went to see Mate Boban in Grude, so let's look at the next two documents on that. They are 4D456 and 4D457. Tell us, please, General, do these two documents have anything to do with your stay with Mate Boban in Grude on that day, the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, they are connected to that. I helped Mr. Boban in compiling this document and in dovetailing it with the other side, that is to say, with Mr. Izetbegovic. So when you look, you'll see that the two documents are almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at Izetbegovic's order. In point 3, he says that he's going to ask the BH UNPROFOR Command to offer its good services to hold a meeting between you and Sefer Halilovic. Their good offices. Was that meeting actually organised?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the meeting was indeed organised, and Mr. Izetbegovic really did take on the responsibility of contacting General Morillon and organising my departure to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, when did you, in fact, leave for Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left on the 10th, sometime around 1730 hours. The helicopter landed at the UNHCR base near Metkovici, and I was taken by helicopter to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, which is P2461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I have a question just out of curiosity. The two documents, 4D456 and 4D457, are these documents that you obtained, yourself, or are these documents that were disclosed by the Prosecutor under Rule 66 and 68?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot, of course, remember each individual document. But looking at the fact that there is not an ERN number here, then I conclude that we procured the documents and didn't receive them through the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the next document, which is under seal, we won't be mentioning the author of the document in that case. Anyway, General, in this document -- well, it's a confidential document, that's its status, and under point 3 it says that on the 11th, in Kiseljak, there was a meeting between Halilovic and Petkovic, and that they had decided to tour the town of Mostar together, and that you and Mr. Halilovic were escorted by General Morillon and other international representatives. And then -- well, tell us, was it on the 11th of May that you had a meeting with Halilovic in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct. On the 11th of May, we did meet in Kiseljak, and General Morillon was present, along with the other representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, is it true and correct, as it says, that on that day, the 11th of May, at 1830 hours, you left Kiseljak together with General Morillon? You and Sefer Halilovic set out towards Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the information is correct. And I'd like to add to that that Mr. Benabou was with us as well. As far as I remember, Mr. Benabou flew in from Kiseljak with us to Metkovic, and then we went towards Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, when did you land in Herzegovina and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not land in Herzegovina. We landed on Croatian territory, the border belt close to the town of Metkovic, which is where the UNHCR had its base, and that's where the helicopters landed generally when they were flying between Kiseljak and Metkovic. And from there, Halilovic and I were transported in an APC belonging to SpaBat. We continued on our journey towards Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, that evening, that is to say, the 11th of May, were you in Grude?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon asked if possible for a brief meeting with Mr. Boban, and from Medjugorje I called Mr. Boban's office. And Mr. Boban received General Morillon straight away, who left for Grude to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, that evening did you have another meeting with Halilovic or not? Did you meet Halilovic again?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned with General Morillon to Medjugorje, and I met Mr. Halilovic briefly. He didn't want to discuss anything before the next day and asked to stay there for the night and talk to Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, how come Arif Pasalic was in this group of people?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we were on the move from Metkovic towards Medjugorje, in the border belt in Bosnia-Herzegovina there's a place called Dracevo, and that's where there was a base for transport or a reinforcement unit to SpaBat. So he we stopped there for a while - I don't know why we stopped - and two minutes later the column continued on its way towards Metkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, was that on the return from Kiseljak on the 11th of May, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the return journey from Kiseljak. We flew by helicopter, and then at the place where the helicopter landed we transferred to an UNPROFOR vehicle and went on our way to their base -- to Medjugorje. And along the way, at Dracevo, we spent a few minutes there. I didn't know why we stopped off there until I reached Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what did you see in Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Halilovic and I were getting out of the APC, and then we saw an APC behind us, and Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Pasalic were coming out of that APC. And that meant that they had joined us when we stopped off by Dracevo. They must have joined us at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you learn anything about how come Pasalic and Filipovic were at Dracevo in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was rather a busy evening at the UNPROFOR place, especially on Mr. Halilovic's part. Well, he learnt that Pasalic had come from Jablanica, through East Mostar, and ended up in Dracevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Halilovic, or anybody else on the Muslim side, did he complain to you at all or to anybody else in the HVO with respect to Mr. Pasalic's being in Dracevo?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't transporting Halilovic for him to complain -- or, rather, Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now a question about the 11th of May. General, I assume you remember General Praljak, during his testimony, mentioning a meeting on that same day to discuss whether the HVO should leave Mostar or not. Do you remember that part of General Praljak's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do remember that part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you know about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I could not have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, after the meeting did anybody inform you of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learnt about the meeting, about what General Praljak presented here, I learnt about that on the 13th or 14th. That's when the stories began going around about what happened during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean the incident that General Praljak described?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I don't want to speak further of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to the next day, the 12th of May. Where were you, General, on that day, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 12th of May, from 8.00 onwards, I was at the base in Medjugorje of SpaBat together with Mr. Halilovic and UNPROFOR representatives. We were working on the finalisation of a joint agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's look at document P2344, and tell us, please, is that the agreement that you and Halilovic reached in the presence of General Morillon and Mr. Thebault? Is that the one you signed on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, was that the operationalisation of the agreement that Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic had reached on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why we were sent for talks to Kiseljak. But in Kiseljak, we didn't manage to reach an agreement about all the details, and General Morillon suggested that the best thing would be for us to go to Herzegovina and Medjugorje straight away. And that's why the meeting in Kiseljak was interrupted and we returned to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I'm now going to ask you to give us an explanation with respect to that agreement. In Article 1 of the agreement, it says what the civilian police should do, the tasks of the civilian police. In Article 4 of the agreement, Article 4 deals with the release of prisoners and the exchange of prisoners of war. Article 5 deals with the return of displaced persons, the return to their homes of displaced persons. General, can you explain to us how you, as the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, came to sign an agreement which has to do with the civilian police, exchanges of prisoners, the release of civilians, and the return of displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason for that is a simple one. All these matters were put before General Morillon as subjects for discussion, and for my part, on the part of the HVO, I had the authority to sign an agreement on behalf of the HVO, regardless of which segments of the agreement were being dealt with. Similarly, Mr. Halilovic, for his part, had this authority. And the commander of UNPROFOR, himself, did not like to have large delegations and mixed delegations to negotiate with. What he wanted was to have a person come in who would be able to sign the agreement at the highest level and that it would be binding on the part of all those mentioned and all those who appeared, and that's how these agreements were signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, as far as the implementation of the agreement was concerned, the section relating to the civilian police, the exchange of prisoners, the release of civilians, the return of displaced persons, did you, as the chief of the Main Staff, and the Main Staff in general, play a role there, or were these affairs dealt with by the competent authorities and organs for the individual areas?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these questions were delegated to those who were -- whose job it was to become acquainted with the agreement and to implement it further.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, would you single out a day in May 1993 as being the day when the situation in Mostar calmed down?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could say that after this agreement and after the establishment of communications between the 4th Corps and the operative zone -- and Halilovic came to Mostar on the 13th, and then -- or on the 14th, to show our goodwill, we organised convoys of humanitarian aid from one side to another, and both of us turned up in Mostar with everybody else. And that's when the situation changed significantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, did you have information about the release of civilians who were evacuated to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information that as soon as this order entered into force, individual groups were being released depending on the security of the facilities to which -- or, rather, the buildings to which they were returning. I believe it was on the 19th of May when all civilians were released and returned, always referring to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In accordance with information that was at your disposal, how would you assess the situation in and around Mostar until the end of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That situation, well, it had its ups and downs. It could happen sometimes that there was brief fighting in an area. There could also be provocations. But in spite of all that, I would say that the situation was under control throughout that time, although there were some indications that the ABiH would try to attack the wider area of Mostar from the north. I would like to mention that the communication between the operative zone and the corps was rather good, although there were interruptions, and I would say the situation was under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you would have to characterise the situation in a word or two, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was almost stable, with sporadic incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are now done with the 9th of May in Mostar, should you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I've been dying to ask a question for the last four years on this document, P2344, because I believe that it is an important document. Since you are one of the four signatories, perhaps you could answer some of my questions. First of all, this document was drafted by Ambassador Thebault and General Morillon, or was it drafted by you and General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document was drafted by the operative staff of the SpaBat, and they would show it to us to be able to make comments or remarks. After the proposals by Mr. Morillon and Mr. Thebault and our amendments, they drafted the final version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're giving us information that I was not aware of. You're saying that it was drafted by the operative staff of the SpaBat, who drafted this document, and this document was presented to yourself and to General Halilovic. So if I understand correctly, you have not drafted the various articles of this document. There are six articles in this document. It is someone from the Spanish Battalion; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we discussed every article, and then the operative staff of the SpaBat drafted the final version. You can tell, by the style of this document, that it doesn't really match the style Halilovic and I used, which was the JNA style. It was very brief and concise, whereas our style was more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The officer from the Spanish Battalion, I was wondering whether he was conversant in three languages, namely, Spanish, his native tongue, English, as well as B/C/S, because both documents are signed in English and in your language, but not in Spanish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the SpaBat had four or five translators who spoke excellent English and excellent Spanish, translators or interpreters, so there was communication in English, and General Morillon and Mr. Thebault understood that, and there was communication in Spanish, which of course the Spanish would understand, and that was interpreted into a language Mr. Halilovic and I understood. So there was interpretation; not of the type that's used here, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering whether yourself, within the HVO, you had a legal expert who oversaw this document, or did you trust the officer from the Spanish Battalion, as well as General Morillon and Mr. Thebault and Mr. Halilovic? Did you have someone going through this document from a legal point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the question again. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering, General Petkovic, whether before you signed the document, you got some advice from a legal expert from the Main Staff or advice from a legal expert from -- a Croat legal expert as to the implications of this document, or did you entirely trust the Spaniards, as well as General Morillon, and Ambassador Thebault, and General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't have any advisers. There were only the two of us, and we accepted what was put on paper. Of course, we made some corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm asking you this question because of Article 4. It says that both parties agree to the immediate release of all civilian detainees, without any conditions, and to be fully completed on the 13th of May, 1993. I was wondering whether you understood, by signing this document, that the signatories acknowledged that civilians were detained, or did you not really realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that time we didn't understand it the same way it is understood today. We knew that people were being taken away and put up someplace else, but we didn't see them as prisoners or detainees. But there were also other aspects. General Halilovic demanded that it be phrased in the document in this very manner, and then a big discussion ensued, whereas I demanded that it be phrased differently. But then both of us accepted what they put on paper, and that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two French nationals who were there, and I hope that they had some legal knowledge, because you do not become a general without knowing a bit about the law, those two people were a witness, and they signed. And this puzzles me greatly, but they signed. Did they not say anything about Article 4? Did it seem perfectly normal to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. The article was put to us in this form, and all four of us signed it, and we immediately launched the implementation to the extent possible. Quite frankly, nobody gave great consideration to any individual phrase in this agreement, because we had no such expert in our ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I was wondering who looked for the various references in the preamble. It talks about the 12th of August, 1949. It talks about the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, and so on and so forth. I was wondering who did the research to find all those documents, because whoever drafted this document had some legal knowledge, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is precisely why I'm saying that this was done by the members of the international forces, because, in principle, all their documents that we signed began or had an introduction like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said earlier on, but -- I don't really speak your language, but for a few words, and I can't really tell the difference, but you said that there were differences between the B/C/S version and the English version. When you said that, I assumed that you had something in mind. So which differences were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot compare the translation with the English version, which was considered official. I accepted the translation as it was, without really knowing what the official version was, and that was the English language version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm surprised. You say that the official version was the English version. I did not see anything to that effect. We have two documents signed by four people, and they seem to carry the same weight. So why are you saying that the English version was the official one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we signed both the English version and the Croatian or Bosnian version. We signed both linguistic versions, and we took the version that we understood with us, whereas the internationals took the English version, so that actually we put our signatures on two original documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, I do not see the header, because it's not very well printed. It says: "Concluded between General Petkovic and General Halilovic." But in the English version, I do not see what is on top. Could you perhaps tell me what it says in the header? It starts with: "Sporazumme" in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Agreement about the cessation of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, concluded between General Milivoj Petkovic and General Sefer Halilovic, on the 12th of May, 1993, in the presence of Lieutenant General Philippe Morillon and Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this contribution, because in the English version I could not read the beginning. One last question in this document, and I will not come back to this because we will have discussed it at length. I was wondering why the drafters of this document did not mention that you were chief of staff of the HVO, and why did it not mention that Mr. Halilovic had a certain function or role? Was doesn't it say "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina"? Why does it say "Territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and so on and so forth? I could spend a lot of time asking you all these various points. So I was wondering why there was no explicit wording stating that it was an agreement signed within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina between two military authorities, yourself and General Halilovic, while, in fact, there is your name, but, in a way, we don't really know who you are, and we don't know whether you are from the ABiH or from the HVO. Someone who discovered this document for the first time would not really know who you are. So do you think that this was done on purpose, or do you think that it was drafted very quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I don't think that that was done on purpose, to leave out anything, or anything like that, because the creator of the introductory part of the document wrote it that way. We saw that it was an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. We saw our names mentioned, Halilovic and I, and we saw who else was present, and we just went ahead and signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. One last question, final question. This document seems to mention very clearly the Vance-Owen Plan, because it is mentioned in the document in Article 1. I was wondering why it was not mentioned in this document that it would be c.c.'d to Mr. Vance, Lord Owen, and so on and so forth. Why do you think it was not necessary to c.c. that or to have this sort of mention? Do you think that there is some sort of a reason? Or perhaps there is no reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti Your Honour, I think that the UNPROFOR command sent on a regular basis reports of this kind or agreements of this kind to Lord Owen. They forwarded it to him; and his military adviser, Brigadier Wilson, would take over these agreements. All agreements signed in Bosnia-Herzegovina would end up in Mr. Owen's office, in the Vance-Owen office, regardless of the fact that it didn't specifically say so here, because they were, of course, very interested in calming the situation down in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have 10 minutes before the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd first of all like to put the transcript right. On page 79, line 21, the verb "to leave" was recorded, whereas I used the verb "to attack." It was about the meeting of the 11th of May that General Praljak testified about, so to avoid misunderstanding in my interpretation of that. Now, our next area is the 30th of June, 1993, Your Honours, a key area in this trial which marks the beginning of total war, the isolation of Muslim soldiers of the HVO, and the arrest of military-able men of Muslim ethnicity. I think it would be more useful if we were to broach the topic tomorrow, to deal with it tomorrow. But if you wish me to start this evening, I'll do my best to organise myself accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are fully right. And, in fact, given that the clock is slightly behind - it's actually much later than it says on the clock - just in order to give us food for thought over night, General Petkovic, I was wondering whether you agreed with what Ms. Alaburic said; namely, that as far as she's concerned - but I'm sure it's the same for you, and this will be noted in the transcript - the 30th of June, 1993, is the most important date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you agree with what she said. I don't quite know how long Ms. Alaburic took. The Registrar will tell us that tomorrow, but for once we are not in a rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you probably have less than two hours. So we are done for the day, and we will resume tomorrow at 2.15. And I wish everyone a very good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
